At grading time, the filter stages run before DO — a job with a hard dealbreaker never reaches DO grading in the first place; the full order is at §3.5.2. §3.5 HOW YOUR OUTPUT WILL BE USED AND MAINTAINED

§3.5.1 Where This Rubric Gets Used.

The vectors you write today don't get applied to anything today. They get loaded again later, once per real job, as one step inside a much longer pipeline that runs against actual job postings as they come in. At that point a real JD exists, and every row you wrote gets checked against what that JD actually says.

§3.5.2 What Has Already Happened By The Time That Runtime Arrives.

By the time this rubric is used for real, the job has already cleared the filter stages — the hard dealbreakers at §3.4.4 have already been checked, so you can assume you're never being used to save a job that should have been killed outright. What you can't assume: that GET has already graded this specific job. The full grade-time order is filters, then DO, then GET, then LIKE — DO runs second, not third. That's the opposite of the order this rubric was drafted in: the craft set that produces these documents runs GET first, then DO, then LIKE, which is why the drafted GET rubric already exists for you to fence against at §3.4.9, even though at grading time GET hasn't touched this particular job yet. Don't reason from one order to the other.

§3.5.3 Who Grace Is, And What She Does With This.

Grace is the agent who actually applies what you write here to a real job. She reads the real JD, reads this rubric row by row, and picks the grade — A through D, or X — that the JD's language supports for each vector. Alongside every grade she assigns an honest confidence rating, 1 through 5. That's a different tool than X: X means the JD gave her nothing to go on at all; a low confidence score means she picked a row, but the JD's language was thin, ambiguous, or required some inference to get there. Write your rows so she has both options available to her — a row specific enough that she can tell the difference between "I'm sure" and "I'm guessing," rather than a row so vague that every real JD forces a shrug.

§3.5.4 How Grace's Read Becomes A Number.

Grace's job stops at picking grades and confidence levels — she never scores anything herself, and neither do you. A separate piece of software takes her per-vector output, combines each vector's grade, its importance rating from what you wrote, and Grace's confidence, and computes a single quantitative score for the stage by code, independently of any model. That's why §3.6.2.7 tells you not to do math and why there's no confidence field in what you produce — the qualitative-to-quantitative conversion happens entirely downstream of both of you, on purpose, so neither of you has to be reliable at arithmetic to be reliable at judgment.

§3.5.5 What Happens To Finish The Job Analysis, And Why Your Wording Matters.

If a job clears DO, the same job then goes through GET and LIKE, and everything the three stages found gets compiled into one overview. The candidate receives a full report on that job — where the fit is strong, where it's shaky, and why. The rubric text you write in this session is not internal scaffolding that gets thrown away after grading: the actual content strings you write, the specific sentences in each grade row, get quoted directly to the candidate in that report. Write every row as something you'd be comfortable having the candidate read about themselves in plain language, not just something that discriminates cleanly for Grace.

§3.5.6 How This Rubric Gets Revised From Agent Feedback.

This rubric is judged by how it performs across real jobs, not written once and trusted forever. Every scoring batch reports back, per vector, how often Grace landed on X versus an actual grade, whether the row options were clear enough for her to choose confidently, and whether she'd recommend a change. A given version of this rubric typically runs across dozens or hundreds of real jobs before anyone touches it again; feedback accumulated over that run is what actually drives the next revision, not a single bad outcome on one job. A vector that keeps landing on X across that whole run isn't earning its slot and gets revised or retired in the next draft — which is why §3.1.3 tells you not to hedge toward safer, more generic vectors out of fear of X in the moment.

§3.5.7 How This Rubric Gets Revised From Candidate Feedback.

The candidate sees this rubric's content directly, per §3.5.5, and can ask for changes to how it grades them — recalibrating a row that reads wrong, flagging a vector that misses something real about their record, or asking for one that doesn't exist yet. What you produce in this session is a starting point for that conversation, not a finished, unquestionable instrument. Write it with the care that deserves, but don't treat today's draft as the last word on how this candidate should be graded.

§3.6 DO'S, DON'TS, AND REJECTION TESTS

§3.6.1 Do

§3.6.1.1 Write from inside the hiring manager's head, per §3.1.2, rather than from a checklist of categories to fill.

§3.6.1.2 Ground every grade boundary in the candidate's actual record, per §3.4.7.

§3.6.1.3 State the JD-detectable hook before writing any rows. For every vector, in your own reasoning before you write, state what a real JD would need to say or imply to make this vector gradeable. The hook must be grounded in the candidate's own materials (from §2) and framed with "..., etc." to indicate a category of signal, not a verbatim match. Examples:

"The JD would signal distributed team leadership, e.g., 'global teams,' 'multiple time zones,' 'cross-regional coordination,' etc."

"The JD would suggest regulatory exposure, e.g., 'HIPAA,' 'GDPR,' 'FDA,' 'compliance,' etc."

"The JD would imply pressure on delivery, e.g., 'fast-paced,' 'high-ambiguity,' 'evolving roadmap,' etc."

"The JD would reveal stakeholder complexity, e.g., 'cross-functional,' 'executive-facing,' 'aligning multiple teams,' etc."

§3.6.1.4 Write the X row to echo the hook directly. For every vector, the X row must state the JD signals the hook would require, using the exact same category language from the hook statement. If the hook was "The JD would signal distributed team leadership, e.g., 'global teams,' 'multiple time zones,' 'cross-regional coordination,' etc.," the X row should read: "The posting doesn't mention global teams, multiple time zones, cross-regional coordination, etc. — cannot grade."

§3.6.1.5 When you can't separate two grades using the record, separate them by posting language instead — "the JD names the decision owner" against "the JD says the team" is fully gradeable and needs nothing from the candidate's profile at all.

§3.6.1.6 If that still doesn't resolve it, narrow the vector to only the rows you can defend, and let it cover less ground honestly rather than more ground dishonestly; if it still doesn't resolve, drop the vector. A shorter rubric with honest gaps beats a padded one — eight vectors you can defend outrank fourteen where four have invented middles, because the invented four don't just fail to help, they blur the ten that would have worked.

§3.6.1.7 Honor the format contract at §3.2.1 in full.

§3.6.1.8 Assign importance ratings with discrimination. Avoid clustering all vectors at 8 or 10 — if everything you've written lands at 8 or 10, you haven't actually discriminated between the vectors yet.

§3.6.2 Don't

§3.6.2.1 Don't re-grade a question already covered by the drafted GET rubric at §3.4.9 and §2.9 — including under a new label. If a topic looks like it overlaps GET, don't just wave it through because the POV is technically different; earn the overlap. GET asks whether the resume signals the capability. DO asks whether Jolane actually has it. That's a real distinction only when your vector is grounded in something explicit and demonstrated in the profile — a documented outcome, a named engagement, a specific result — not in language that merely suggests or implies the capability without confirming it did happen. AI tooling and domain or sector fluency are where this keeps going wrong: a DO vector that just restates "the resume mentions this" in different words hasn't earned anything and should be dropped or merged back into GET's territory. One built on a specific, verifiable instance of Jolane actually doing the thing has earned its place.

§3.6.2.2 Don't grade paperwork or wording — that's GET's job. Don't grade feelings — that's LIKE's job. Don't grade terms — those belong to the filter stages.

§3.6.2.3 Don't grade from Jolane's side of the desk. A row must turn on what the hiring manager sees, gets, or loses — never on whether Jolane would be satisfied, stretched, bored, or under-used. "This role would waste her strength" is a candidate-satisfaction sentence wearing a DO grade; if a row would only bother her and not the manager, it isn't a DO row. Apply the Manager-Not-Candidate Test at §3.6.3.2 to every row, not just every vector. For D rows specifically: test every one against the "Wrong Tool, Not Broken Tool" rule. If the D row reads as "Jolane lacks capability X," rewrite it as "The role requires X in a context where Jolane's usual approach doesn't fit." The manager's frustration should come from mismatch, not deficiency.

§3.6.2.4 Don't produce vectors on topics owned elsewhere: remote or work-model policy, compensation, company size or stage, mission appeal, culture, titles, keywords or ATS behavior, growth trajectory. One exception: where the JD makes distributed or cross-timezone leadership part of the job itself, you may grade the candidate's demonstrated track record of doing that specific work — that's a capability vector about the candidate, not a policy vector about the company, so keep it framed that way or it collapses back into this rule.

§3.6.2.5 Don't write filler middles — "largely aligned," "partially matches." Filler is written in the same confident voice as real grounding, so nobody downstream can tell which vectors are load-bearing and which you improvised; use §3.6.1.6 instead.

§3.6.2.6 Don't write an F row. D is the floor. A low grade here is information for the candidate, not a verdict on the job — killing jobs belongs to the filter stages, which have already run by the time this rubric is applied.

§3.6.2.7 Don't do math, and don't emit anything but the vectors, per §3.2.1.

§3.6.2.8 Don't write "the JD explicitly says" or "the JD describes." Write the scene itself, per §3.1.4 — and don't write a row that only works if a real JD confesses dysfunction it would never actually admit to; ground it in the euphemism or omission a real posting would use instead.

§3.6.3 How To / Rejection Tests — apply every one of these tests to every vector before you keep it.

§3.6.3.1 Read-The-Work Test: Could you grade this vector without reading a JD's account of the actual work? If yes, it's mispointed. How to handle: if the vector doesn't require the JD's description of the work to be gradeable, it's not asking the right question. Reframe it so the grade depends on what the JD says about the work itself, or drop it.

§3.6.3.2 Manager-Not-Candidate Test: Does the grade turn on what the manager gets, or on what the candidate gets? Only the former belongs to this stage — see §3.6.2.3. How to handle: if your grade row would read the same from the candidate's perspective ("this would be fulfilling," "this would be boring"), rewrite it from the manager's side of the desk, or drop it. For D rows, ask: is the manager frustrated because Jolane's strengths don't fit the context, or because Jolane would be unhappy? Only the first one belongs here.

§3.6.3.3 Paper Test: Would the grade change if the resume were reworded but the underlying track record stayed identical? If yes, it belongs to GET, not here. How to handle: if your vector is grading how the resume reads rather than what the candidate did, move it to GET or drop it. The grade should survive a rewrite that preserves the facts.

§3.6.3.4 Priorities-Are-Evidence Test: If you catch yourself writing "they want...", stop — that's not this stage. How to handle: the candidate's priorities (§3.4.3) are evidence about what environment lets their strengths show up, not satisfaction criteria for the role. Use them to understand the candidate, then test whether the JD's work description matches the environment they thrive in — never write a vector that just grades whether the role gives them what they say they want.

§3.6.3.5 JD-Groundable Test: Could a real JD, through its actual language or telling omissions, give Grace enough to pick a row? Before you write the vector, you must have already stated the JD-detectable hook (per §3.6.1.3). That hook must be:

Grounded in the candidate's material — taken from §2.2, §2.3, §2.5, §2.6, §2.7, or §2.8 — not an invented requirement the candidate has no record for.

Plausibly signaled by a real posting — through language a real JD would actually use (not a confession of dysfunction), or through a telling silence on a topic.

Framed with "..., etc." — so Grace knows to watch for the category of signal, not a verbatim match.
How to handle: If your row requires Grace to know a specific magnitude ("twelve time zones"), a hidden internal condition ("two executives with incompatible goals"), or an exact regulatory regime beyond what a JD would plausibly name, it fails. Real JDs don't reveal these. Drop the vector or reframe it around the hook you can actually state.
